title: Chapter 6 — Judicial Power In The United States
paragraphs: Judicial Power in the United States and Its Influence on Political Society.

I thought it essential to devote a separate chapter to the judicial authorities of the United States. If I mentioned them only in passing, their great political importance might be lessened in the reader’s eyes. Confederations have existed in other countries besides America, and republics have been established on more than the shores of the New World. Several States of Europe have adopted the representative system of government. But I am not aware that any nation in the world has so far organized a judicial power on the principle the Americans now follow. The judicial organization of the United States is the institution a foreigner has the most difficulty understanding. He hears the authority of a judge invoked in the political events of every day, and he naturally concludes that in the United States judges are important political officials. Yet when he examines the nature of the courts, he finds nothing contrary to the usual habits and privileges of such bodies, and the judges seem to him to interfere in public affairs only by chance — but by a chance that recurs every day.

When the Parliament of Paris remonstrated, refused to register an edict, or summoned an official accused of misconduct in office to its bar, its political influence as a judicial body was plainly visible. Nothing of the kind is to be seen in the United States. The Americans have kept all the ordinary characteristics of judicial authority and have carefully confined its action to the ordinary circle of its functions.

The first characteristic of judicial power in all nations is the duty of arbitration. But for a tribunal to intervene, rights must be contested, and a lawsuit must be brought to obtain a judge’s decision. As long as the law is uncontested, therefore, the judicial authority is not called on to discuss it, and it may exist without being noticed. When a judge, in a given case, attacks a law relating to that case, he extends the circle of his customary duties without stepping beyond it, because he is to some extent obliged to rule on the law in order to rule on the case. But if he pronounces on a law without resting on a case, he clearly steps outside his sphere and invades that of the legislative authority.

The second characteristic of judicial power is that it rules on particular cases, not on general principles. Suppose a judge, in deciding a particular point, destroys a general principle. His judgment tends to reject all the inferences from that principle and so to annul it, yet he remains within the ordinary limits of his functions. But if he attacks a general principle directly, without having a particular case in view, he leaves the circle in which all nations have agreed to confine his authority. He assumes a more important, and perhaps more useful, influence than that of a magistrate, but he ceases to represent the judicial power.

The third characteristic of the judicial power is that it cannot act unless it is appealed to, or until it has taken up a matter. This characteristic is less general than the other two. But despite the exceptions, I think it may be regarded as essential. By its nature the judicial power has no action of its own; it must be set in motion to produce a result. When it is called on to repress a crime, it punishes the criminal. When a wrong is to be redressed, it is ready to redress it. When an act requires interpretation, it is prepared to interpret it. But it does not pursue criminals, hunt out wrongs, or examine evidence of its own accord. A judicial official who opened proceedings on his own and usurped the censorship of the laws would to some extent do violence to the passive nature of his authority.

The Americans have kept these three distinguishing characteristics of the judicial power. An American judge can pronounce a decision only when litigation has arisen. He deals only with particular cases. And he cannot act until the case has been duly brought before the court. His position is therefore exactly like that of the magistrate in other nations, and yet he is invested with immense political power. If the sphere of his authority and his means of action are the same as those of other judges, one may ask where he gets a power they do not have. The cause of the difference lies in a simple fact: the Americans have acknowledged the right of judges to base their decisions on the constitution rather than on the laws. In other words, they have left judges free not to apply laws that seem to them unconstitutional.

I am aware that courts in other countries have claimed a similar right, but claimed it in vain. In America, however, all authorities recognize it, and no party, not even a single individual, is found to contest it. This fact can be explained only by the principles of the American constitution. In France the constitution is (or at least is supposed to be) immutable, and the received theory is that no power has the right to change any part of it. In England Parliament has an acknowledged right to modify the constitution. Since the constitution can therefore undergo perpetual changes, it does not in reality exist; Parliament is at once a legislative and a constituent assembly. The political theories of America are simpler and more rational. An American constitution is not supposed to be immutable, as in France, nor can the ordinary powers of society modify it, as in England. It forms a separate whole. Because it represents the determination of the whole people, it is no less binding on the legislator than on the private citizen. But the will of the people may alter it, in predetermined cases, according to established rules. In America, then, the constitution may change, but as long as it exists it is the origin of all authority and the sole vehicle of the predominant force. *a

a [ [The fifth article of the original Constitution of the United States lays down how amendments to the Constitution may be made. Two-thirds of both Houses of Congress must propose an amendment, and the legislatures of three-fourths of the several States must ratify it. Fifteen amendments have been made at different times since 1789. The most important are the Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth, which were framed and ratified after the Civil War. The original Constitution of the United States, followed by these fifteen amendments, is printed at the end of this edition. — Translator’s Note, 1874.]]

It is easy to see how these differences must affect the position and the rights of the judicial bodies in the three countries I have cited. Suppose the tribunals in France were authorized to disobey laws on the ground that they conflict with the constitution. The supreme power would in fact be placed in their hands, since they alone would have the right to interpret a constitution whose clauses no authority can modify. They would therefore take the place of the nation and exercise as absolute a sway over society as the inherent weakness of judicial power would allow. Undoubtedly, because French judges are not competent to declare a law unconstitutional, the power to change the constitution is indirectly given to the legislative body, since no legal barrier would oppose the alterations it might prescribe. But it is better to grant the power to change the people’s constitution to men who represent (however imperfectly) the will of the people than to men who represent no one but themselves.

It would be still more unreasonable to give English judges the right to resist the decisions of the legislative body, since the Parliament that makes the laws also makes the constitution. Consequently a law that emanates from the three powers of the State can in no case be unconstitutional. But neither of these remarks applies to America.

In the United States the constitution binds the legislator just as it binds the private citizen. It is the first of laws, so it cannot be modified by a law, and it is only right that the courts should obey the constitution in preference to any law. The power of the judiciary depends on this condition, because every magistrate has a natural right to choose the legal obligation that binds him most strictly.

In France the constitution is also the first of laws, and judges have the same right to take it as the ground of their decisions. But if they exercised this right, they would inevitably encroach on rights more sacred than their own, namely those of society, in whose name they act. In that case the motive of the State clearly prevails over the motives of an individual. In America the nation can always bring its magistrates to obedience by changing its constitution, so no danger of this kind is to be feared. On this point, therefore, the political and the logical reasons agree, and the people as well as the judges keep their privileges.

Whenever a law that the judge holds to be unconstitutional is argued in a court of the United States, he may refuse to accept it as a rule. This power is the only one peculiar to the American magistrate, but it gives rise to immense political influence. Few laws can escape the searching analysis of the judicial power for long, for there are few that do not harm some private interest or other, and none that cannot be brought before a court, whether by the choice of the parties or by the necessity of the case. But from the moment a judge has refused to apply a given law in a case, that law loses some of its moral force. The people whose interests it harms learn that ways exist of evading its authority, and similar suits multiply until the law becomes powerless. One of two alternatives must then be taken: the people must alter the constitution, or the legislature must repeal the law. The political power the Americans have entrusted to their courts is therefore immense. But the evils of this power are considerably reduced by the obligation to attack laws only through the courts. Suppose the judge had been empowered to contest laws on the ground of theoretical generalities, or to open an attack or pass a censure on the legislator. He would then have played a prominent part in the political sphere, and as the champion or the antagonist of a party he would have drawn the hostile passions of the nation into the conflict. But when a judge contests a law applied to some particular case in an obscure proceeding, the importance of his attack is hidden from the public gaze. His decision bears on the interest of an individual, and if the law is slighted, it is only indirectly. Moreover, although the law is censured, it is not abolished. Its moral force may be diminished, but its binding force is by no means suspended, and its final destruction can be accomplished only by the repeated attacks of judicial officials. It is easy to understand that legislation is protected from wanton assailants and from the daily aggressions of party spirit, because the censorship of the laws is tied to the private interests of members of the community and the prosecution of the law is intimately joined to the prosecution of an individual. The errors of the legislator are exposed when their evil consequences are most felt, and the basis of a prosecution is always a positive, appreciable fact.

I am inclined to believe that this practice of the American courts is at once the most favorable to liberty and to public order. If the judge could attack the legislator only openly and directly, he would sometimes be afraid to offer any resistance to the legislator’s will. At other moments party spirit might encourage him to defy it at every turn. The laws would consequently be attacked when the power they come from is weak, and obeyed when it is strong. That is to say, they would be contested when it would be useful to respect them, and respected when it would be easy to turn them into an instrument of oppression. But the American judge is brought into the political arena independently of his own will. He judges the law only because he is obliged to judge a case. The political question he is called on to resolve is connected with the interest of the parties to the suit, and he cannot refuse to decide it without abdicating the duties of his post. He performs his duties as a citizen by fulfilling the precise duties that belong to his profession as a magistrate. It is true that under this system the judicial censorship the courts exercise over legislation cannot extend to all laws indiscriminately. Some laws can never give rise to the exact kind of contest called a lawsuit, and even when such a contest is possible, it may happen that no one cares to bring it before a court. The Americans have often felt this disadvantage, but they have left the remedy incomplete, lest they give it an efficacy that might in some cases prove dangerous. Within these limits, the power of American courts to pronounce a statute unconstitutional forms one of the most powerful barriers ever devised against the tyranny of political assemblies.
Other Powers Granted to American Judges

In the United States all citizens have the right to indict public officials before the ordinary courts — How they use this right — Article 75 of the French Constitution of the Year VIII — The Americans and the English cannot understand the meaning of this clause.

It is perfectly natural that in a free country like America all citizens should have the right to indict public officials before the ordinary courts, and that all judges should have the power to punish public offenses. The right granted to the courts to judge the agents of the executive government when they have violated the laws is so natural that it cannot be seen as an extraordinary privilege. Nor do the springs of government seem to me weakened in the United States by the custom of making all public officers answerable to the judges of the land. On the contrary, the Americans seem by this means to have increased the respect due to the authorities, and at the same time to have made those in power more careful not to offend public opinion. I was struck by the small number of political trials in the United States, but I had no difficulty accounting for it. A lawsuit, of whatever kind, is always a difficult and expensive undertaking. It is easy to attack a public man in a newspaper, but the motives that can warrant an action at law must be serious. A solid ground of complaint must therefore exist before an individual will prosecute a public officer, and public officers take care not to furnish such grounds when they are afraid of being prosecuted.

This does not come from the republican form of American institutions, since the same facts are found in England. Neither nation regards the impeachment of the principal officers of State as enough to guarantee its independence. Both hold that the right to bring minor prosecutions, which the whole community can reach, is a better pledge of freedom than those great judicial actions, which are rarely used until it is too late.

In the Middle Ages offenders were very hard to catch, and judges inflicted the most dreadful tortures on the few who were arrested. This did nothing to reduce the number of crimes. People have since discovered that justice is more effective when it is both more certain and more mild. The English and the Americans hold that tyranny and oppression should be treated like any other crime: lighten the penalty and make conviction easier.

In the Year VIII of the French Republic a constitution was drawn up that included the following clause: “Art. 75. All the agents of the government below the rank of ministers can only be prosecuted for offenses relating to their several functions by virtue of a decree of the Conseil d’Etat; in which case the prosecution takes place before the ordinary tribunals.” This clause outlasted the “Constitution de l’An VIII,” and it is still maintained in spite of the just complaints of the nation. I have always had the utmost difficulty explaining its meaning to Englishmen or Americans. They at once concluded that the Conseil d’Etat in France was a great tribunal, established in the center of the kingdom, exercising a preliminary and somewhat tyrannical jurisdiction in all political cases. But when I told them that the Conseil d’Etat was not a judicial body in the common sense of the term, but an administrative council made up of men dependent on the Crown, so that the king, after ordering one of his servants, called a Prefect, to commit an injustice, has the power to command another of his servants, called a Councillor of State, to prevent the first from being punished; when I showed them that a citizen injured by the sovereign’s order is obliged to ask the sovereign for permission to obtain redress, they refused to believe so flagrant an abuse and were tempted to accuse me of falsehood or ignorance. Before the Revolution it often happened that a Parliament issued a warrant against a public officer who had committed an offense, and sometimes the proceedings were stopped by the authority of the Crown, which enforced compliance with its absolute and despotic will. It is painful to see how much lower we have sunk than our forefathers, since we allow to pass, under the color of justice and the sanction of the law, things that only violence could impose.
